Heritage sites by state

Heritage sites in Assam: Moidams, Sivasagar and Majuli

Assam has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the Moidams of Charaideo, the mound burials of the Ahom kings (2024), and the Kaziranga and Manas national parks. Its other major heritage sites include Ahom Sivasagar, the satras of Majuli, Kamakhya and Madan Kamdev near Guwahati, and the early stone doorway of Da Parbatia at Tezpur.

We design study tours to the Moidams, Sivasagar and Majuli for groups on request, with a lecture before you travel.

Why Assam matters for Indian heritage

Assam sits where the Brahmaputra valley meets the hills of the north-east, and its history reflects both. Early kingdoms known as Kamarupa (roughly the 4th to 12th centuries) built temples in stone and brick and issued copper plate grants in Sanskrit. From 1228 the Ahom dynasty, whose founder Sukaphaa came over the Patkai hills from the Tai world of upper Burma, ruled the eastern valley for about six hundred years until the British annexation of 1826. The Koch, Kachari and Chutiya states were also major powers.

On top of this came the neo-Vaishnava movement of Srimanta Sankardeva (15th to 16th centuries), which created the satras, monastic institutions that still shape music, theatre, dance and crafts. Sattriya, one of India's recognised classical dances, comes from them; it is one of the eight dance forms usually listed as classical.

Heritage walks in this state: Guwahati

Museums in Assam

  • Assam State Museum, Guwahati. Sculpture from Kamarupa sites, inscriptions, manuscripts and ethnographic galleries.
  • Srimanta Sankardeva Kalakshetra, Guwahati. Cultural complex on Assamese arts, crafts and the satra traditions.
  • Charaideo site museum. Context for the Moidams and Ahom burial customs.
  • Tai Ahom Museum, Sivasagar. Objects, manuscripts and arms from the Ahom period.

UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Assam

The Moidams of Charaideo were inscribed in 2024 as the mound-burial system of the Ahom dynasty. Charaideo, the first Ahom capital, holds the royal burial ground: earthen mounds raised over vaulted chambers, where kings and nobles were buried with objects for the afterlife. Many were robbed in the past, and the site is valued as much for its sacred landscape of mounds, ponds and trees as for what was found inside. Our session on burials and bioarchaeology explains how archaeologists study such tombs.

Kaziranga (1985), known for the greater one-horned rhinoceros, and Manas (1985), on the Bhutan border, are natural sites. They belong on a heritage trip because the forest, grassland and river shape where people settled. For the national picture see UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India.

Sivasagar and the Ahom capitals

Sivasagar, the 18th-century Ahom capital of Rangpur, has the densest group of Ahom buildings. The Rang Ghar, an oval two-storey pavilion from the mid-18th century, was a royal stand for watching buffalo fights and games during Bihu. The Talatal Ghar and the Kareng Ghar at nearby Garhgaon are palaces built in brick with a lime and organic mortar. The Sivasagar tank, with the Shiva Dol, Vishnu Dol and Devi Dol on its bank, was built in the 1730s under Queen Ambika.

These buildings are worth reading as political statements. The Ahom rulers kept Tai traditions, including the Buranji chronicles, while adopting Hindu temple patronage, and the temple towers at Sivasagar mix local and north Indian forms.

Majuli and the satras

Majuli, in the Brahmaputra, is one of the largest river islands in the world and the main centre of the satra tradition. Satras such as Auniati, Dakhinpat, Kamalabari and Garamur keep a prayer hall (namghar), resident monks, manuscripts and performance traditions. Samaguri Satra is known for mask making used in bhaona theatre. Majuli is on India's tentative list for UNESCO, which is not the same as being inscribed.

Erosion has reduced the island's area over the last century, and some satras have moved. That makes Majuli a strong case study for the link between heritage and environment, a theme we cover in climate change and ancient settlements.

Ancient temples in Assam

Kamakhya, on Nilachal hill in Guwahati, is a major Shakta temple; the present superstructure was rebuilt in the 16th century under Koch patronage on older foundations. Madan Kamdev, north of Guwahati, is a field of carved stone ruins from around the 10th to 12th centuries. Hajo has the Hayagriva Madhava temple, important to Hindus and Buddhists, and the Poa Mecca mosque. Umananda sits on a small island in the river opposite Guwahati.

At Tezpur, the stone doorframe of Da Parbatia, with river goddesses on its jambs, is usually dated to about the 5th to 6th centuries and is among the oldest sculpture in Assam. Surya Pahar in Goalpara has rock-cut shrines and images linked to Hindu, Buddhist and Jain worship. Our Reading a temple lecture helps groups read these ruins before they visit.

Archaeology and written sources in Assam

Assam is unusual in India for the range of its written sources. Kamarupa kings left copper plate grants in Sanskrit, such as those of Bhaskaravarman in the 7th century, who is also described by the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang. The Ahom court kept Buranjis, chronicles written first in the Tai Ahom language and later in Assamese, which record reigns, wars and court events in detail. Satras preserved manuscripts on sanchi bark, painted and written by hand.

Archaeology adds what these texts leave out. Excavations at Ambari in Guwahati exposed brick structures and pottery from the early medieval centuries, and survey work across the valley keeps finding temple ruins buried by river silt. Floods and earthquakes, including the great earthquake of 1897, have damaged many stone temples, which is why so many sites, Madan Kamdev among them, survive as fields of carved blocks. A museum gallery study at the Assam State Museum works well before seeing these ruins.

Planning a heritage trip in Assam

A practical plan uses two bases. Guwahati covers Kamakhya, Umananda, Hajo, Madan Kamdev and the museums; see our heritage walk in Guwahati guide. Jorhat or Sivasagar covers Charaideo, Sivasagar, Garhgaon and Majuli, with Kaziranga on the way. Ferry timings to Majuli vary with the river, so confirm locally.

We design a study tour for your group around these sites, and families can ask about private journeys.

Questions people ask

How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are there in Assam?

Three. Kaziranga and Manas national parks were inscribed in 1985 as natural sites, and the Moidams of Charaideo, the mound-burial system of the Ahom dynasty, were inscribed in 2024 as a cultural site. Majuli is on the tentative list.

What are the Moidams of Charaideo?

They are royal burial mounds of the Ahom kings and nobles at Charaideo, the first Ahom capital. Each mound covers a vaulted chamber where the dead were placed with objects, and the whole area forms a sacred burial landscape.

What are the main historical places in Sivasagar?

The Rang Ghar, the Talatal Ghar, the Shiva Dol on the Sivasagar tank, the Kareng Ghar at Garhgaon and the nearby Moidams at Charaideo. Together they cover the later centuries of Ahom rule, roughly the 17th and 18th centuries.

Is Majuli a UNESCO World Heritage Site?

No. Majuli is on India's tentative list but has not been inscribed. It is valued for its satras, the neo-Vaishnava monasteries with their music, dance, theatre and mask-making traditions, and for its river island setting.

Can we book a heritage tour of Assam for students?

Yes. Talaash Heritage designs custom study tours on request, usually with Guwahati and Sivasagar or Jorhat as bases, and can add a lecture before the trip on Ahom history, temple architecture or burial archaeology.
